slides.title: The Office — Time Prank
slides.subtitle: Jim pulls one of his classic pranks: he messes with time to drive Dwight crazy.

words.translation: a trick played on someone to make people laugh
words.example: Jim's prank on Dwight was hilarious.

words.translation: a person you work with, especially at the same level
words.example: She had lunch with her coworkers.

words.translation: to tease or annoy someone on purpose, usually for fun
words.example: Jim loves to mess with Dwight.

words.translation: to make someone believe something that is not true
words.example: He tricked his brother into cleaning the room.

words.translation: to see or become aware of something
words.example: Dwight didn't notice that the clock was wrong.

words.translation: to behave as if something is true when it is not
words.example: Jim pretended it was late in the afternoon.

words.translation: making you feel slightly angry or impatient
words.example: Dwight can be very annoying in the office.

words.translation: not interesting or exciting in any way
words.example: Office work can be boring sometimes.

words.translation: the person who is in charge of a company or team
words.example: Michael is the boss of the branch.

words.translation: to understand something after thinking about it
words.example: It took Dwight a while to figure out the prank.

words.word: Jim loves to mess with Dwight during the day.
words.example: Pattern: mess with (someone) = to tease or annoy
Pattern: figure out (something) = to understand after thinking
words.word: Dwight couldn't figure out why the time was moving so fast.

words.example: Pattern: get on with (something) = to continue doing something
words.word: They usually get on with their tasks after lunch.

slides.title: Language Awareness — Phrasal Verbs
slides.content:
Comedies like The Office are full of phrasal verbs — everyday combinations of a verb and a small word (in, out, up, with) that native speakers use constantly. They often have a meaning you cannot guess from the parts alone.
• verb + preposition → the two words act as one unit
• the meaning is often figurative, not literal
• the object usually goes at the end (mess WITH someone, figure OUT the joke)
Notice the phrasal verbs below and pay attention to which small word follows the verb.
